title: One Year and a Day
premise: Marshall Field Jr. possesses a wife, three children, a lavish new wing and the prospect of inheriting the largest fortune in Chicago. On this November afternoon, he has precisely one year and one day remaining.

opening.text:
JAUNT: ONE YEAR AND A DAY. A Monday afternoon, 21 November 1904, at the Field residences on Prairie Avenue.

Four stops between two houses: the patriarch's and the heir's. Marshall Field constructed one of the preeminent department stores of America and accumulated the largest fortune in Chicago. His only surviving son lives two doors away: thirty-six, affluent, and still anticipating, as he has throughout his existence, the moment he will become his father's equal. Count the days alongside him. Exactly one year and one day from now, a gunshot will reverberate through the residence at 1919.

Begin at the heir's entrance.

stops.text: 1919 Prairie, the residence of Mr. and Mrs. Marshall Field Jr. He acquired the property in 1890, and in 1902 D. H. Burnham and Company constructed "a huge addition" on his behalf. He married Albertine Huck, and they have three children: Henry, Marshall III and the youngest, Gwendolyn. Observe them on the front walk this afternoon, the nurse carrying the infant, the boys bundled in overcoats. Every conceivable advantage is assembled on this walk, excepting his own identity, which remains the property of his father. He has been designated Junior his entire life, and the diminutive has never relaxed its grip. Walk north two doors to the residence where the name genuinely resides.

stage.caption: Marshall Field Jr. and his wife step onto the walk where the nurse waits with their children.

stops.text: 1905 Prairie, the patriarch's mansion, where the heir was raised, "the first in Chicago to be completely wired for electricity". An elder son, Louis, died in infancy; this one survived and was cultivated to inherit the enterprise that instructed America to "Give the lady what she wants". His father is "the wealthiest and most powerful businessman in Chicago", and he relinquishes authority to nobody. Indeed, he intends to transmit it beyond his son altogether: his will is structured to hold the fortune in trust for forty years for the grandsons now playing on the walk at 1919. The heir ascends to his father's entrance for his customary Monday visit, and Benson the butler admits him. The mansion will be demolished in 1955.

stage.caption: Marshall Field Jr. approaches his father's entrance, and Thomas Benson opens the door for him.

stops.text: Farther along the avenue, turn and contemplate both residences. This is what society observes: a dutiful son discharging his obligations. And this is what society murmurs behind its curtains. The Levee district lies three blocks west, where the Everleigh Club on Dearborn Street, the city's most notorious brothel, numbers the wealthiest young men of Chicago among its clientele, and the gossips include Marshall Field Jr. Nobody has substantiated it, and nobody ever will. Nevertheless, a year and a day hence, rumor will crystallize into legend: "The most popular story is that he was in fact shot at the Everleigh Club", then transported home and staged as an accident. Others will maintain it was suicide. Return to 1919.

stage.caption: A gentleman and a lady promenade past the Field residences, and the gentleman inclines his head meaningfully toward 1919.

stops.text: 1919 once more, as the afternoon wanes. The children have retired indoors. On Wednesday, 22 November 1905, precisely one year and a day from this moment, Marshall Field Jr. will be shot within this house, surviving five days. At Mercy Hospital he will insist, "I shot myself with that revolver – accidentally", and the coroner's jury will determine that he "had shot himself unintentionally while examining a revolver". Two reporters will receive anonymous tips that he spent that evening at the Everleigh Club; the proprietors will deny it, and no corroboration will ever emerge. Contemplate the illuminated windows. The son of the wealthiest man in Chicago is home for dinner, with a single year and a day remaining.

stage.caption: A maid draws the curtains at 1919 as daylight diminishes, and the nurse ushers the children indoors.

legs.story: North two doors, past the Moulton residence, to the patriarch's entrance at 1905.
North along the sidewalk to regard both Field residences as the avenue does.
Back south along the sidewalk to 1919, as the gas lamps are illuminated.

endings.text: The walk concludes here. Marshall Field Jr. died at Mercy Hospital on Monday, 27 November 1905. His father, seventy-one and recently remarried, played golf on New Year's Day, contracted pneumonia, and "six weeks later, Marshall Field, Sr. was dead". The fortune, valued at approximately $125 million, passed in trust to the boys from the front walk at 1919, precisely as the will had prescribed: sixty percent to Marshall III and forty percent to Henry. The heir never transcended the designation of Junior; his sons inherited everything, which suggests how thoroughly a dynasty's ambitions could eclipse the individual life lived beneath them.

keepsake.title: The Field Inheritance
keepsake.text: An interpretive card documenting the Field family on Prairie Avenue in 1904; a reconstruction prepared for this walk, not a historical artifact.

evidence.text: Marshall Field Jr. Residence: enlarged and improved several times, the last in 1902, when D. H. Burnham & Company built a huge addition for Marshall Field Jr., who had acquired the property in 1890.
The 1904 Blue Book lists Mr. and Mrs. Marshall Field jr. at 1919 Prairie.
evidence.locator: The street-and-number list, PRAIRIE AV., as data/residents_1904/households/hh_field_marshall_jr.json reads it.

evidence.text: Marshall Field Jr. (1868-1905) married Albertine Huck, and they were the parents of Henry Field, Marshall Field III and Gwendolyn. Field's will held his remaining estate in trust for 40 years for his two grandsons, 60 percent to Marshall Field III and 40 percent to Henry, who died in 1917.

One Year and a Day: the day, Monday 21 November 1904, the hour and the order of the walk are this jaunt's framing, chosen because the stories meet on it (three days after Arthur Caton's death, a Monday of the Reading Class, before Kimball's death in December). No visit on that day is asserted.

One Year and a Day: who is seen at each stop, where they stand, what they do and when are reconstructed. People with cards in the town play themselves; people the town has no card for (and the unnamed servants, callers and passers-by) are unnamed figures in period dress, and no likeness is claimed. No word anyone says is asserted.

Marshall and Nannie Field had three children: Louis, who died in infancy, and Marshall, Jr. and Ethel, raised at 1905 Prairie, 'the first in Chicago to be completely wired for electricity', built in 1876 at a cost of some $2 million.

Marshall Field: 'Give the lady what she wants'; 'the wealthiest and most powerful businessman in Chicago', his fortune valued at $125 million in 1905. His son Marshall Field Jr. was shot on 22 November 1905; Field himself died of pneumonia on 16 January 1906, caught after a New Year's Day golf game with, among others, Robert Todd Lincoln.
evidence.locator: The biography's paragraphs on the store, his wealth, his son and his death.

evidence.text: Marshall Field Residence, 1905 S. Prairie Avenue: later converted to an aeronautical university. Razed 1955.

The census of 1 June 1900 enumerated John Dunford, coachman, born in England, as the head of his own household in the rear building behind 1905 Prairie, and Thomas Benson, butler, born in Ireland, in the house.
'The most popular story is that he was in fact shot at the Everleigh Club', a brothel, and brought home to look like an accident; other accounts say suicide.
evidence.locator: The post's paragraph on the Marshall Field Jr. house.

evidence.text: The blog names actor John Barrymore, authors Ring Lardner and Theodore Dreiser, and Marshall Field, Jr. among the club's famed clients, and says rumours persisted for years that the young Field had been shot there; Wikipedia: 'A rival madam maliciously accused the Everleigh sisters of murdering Field.'
evidence.locator: Other Ladies: the clients paragraph; Wikipedia: Scandals.

evidence.text: On Wednesday 22 November 1905 Marshall Field Jr. was shot at 1919 Prairie, his parents' house next door at 1905; he died at Mercy Hospital on Monday 27 November, saying 'I shot myself with that revolver – accidentally', and the coroner's jury found he 'had shot himself unintentionally while examining a revolver'. Two reporters were tipped that he had spent the evening at the Everleigh Club, 2131-33 S. Dearborn; the sisters denied it and nobody confirmed it.
evidence.locator: The account of the shooting and the rumours.

evidence.text: 'Despite the aid of Chicago's best surgeons, Field died of what the Tribune termed an accidentally self-inflicted gunshot wound. Six weeks later, Marshall Field, Sr. was dead.'

The marriage licence acquired in London in 1905 gave Delia as 46 and Field as 70. They married at St. Margaret's, Westminster; 'The ceremony was quiet, and attended only by a few friends.' Field died in 1906 of pneumonia after a round of golf in a foursome that included Robert Todd Lincoln. Delia was left $1 million and the Field mansion on Prairie Avenue, moved to Washington, D.C., where her house was known as the Pink Palace, and died in 1937.
evidence.locator: Second Mrs. Field: the paragraphs on the marriage and after; Wikipedia: the death on 16 January 1906.
